3.text: takes offence, and leaves the family camp. He goes away to the border-land

4.text: of the Koryak, who assault him in his travelling-tent. He, however, snatches

5.text: his fire-board implement, and with its small bow of antler, shoots the wooden

6.text: drill at his adversaries. Immediately it turns into a fiery shaft and destroys

7.text: all of them one by one. He then takes their herds, and, coming back to

8.text: his home, shows his newly acquired wealth to his relatives, saying, “See now

9.text: what that of woman’s breeches was able to procure for you.”

10.text: Moreover, each “soft man” is supposed to have a special protector

11.text: among the “spirits,” who, for the most part, is said to play the part of a

12.text: supernatural husband, keˊlᴇ-husband (keˊle-uwäˊᵋquč), of the transformed one.

13.text: This husband is supposed to be the real head of the family and to communi-

14.text: cate his orders by means of his transformed wife. The human husband, of

15.text: course, has to execute these orders faithfully under fear of prompt punishment.

16.text: Thus in a household like that, the voice of the wife is decidedly preponderant.

17.text: The husband often takes the name of his wife as an addition to his own

18.text: name; for instance, Têluˊwg̣ê-Yaˊtirg̣ɪn (“Yaˊtirg̣ɪn, husband of Tiluˊwg̣i)”.

19.text: Otherwise the same is done by the children with the name of their father;

21.text: The keˊlᴇ-husband is very sensitive to even the slightest mockery of his

22.text: transformed wife, because he knows that the “soft man” feels exceedingly

23.text: “bashful,” and also because he is doubtless conscious that the position of

24.text: the latter is ridiculed on account of his obedience to his own orders.

25.text: Speaking further of the marriage-relation with supernatural beings, some

26.text: shamans of untransformed sex are said also to have keˊlᴇ-wives, who take

27.text: part in the every-day life of their house. Thus, in the tale of a contest of

28.text: two shamans,¹ one of them is said to have a keˊlᴇ-wife. Her face looks on

29.text: him from the wall of his sleeping-room. Whenever he wants to take a meal,

30.text: his human wife brings him meat and begins to cut it into small pieces.

31.text: He eats them one by one, and during the meal the face of the keˊlᴇ-wife

32.text: keeps watch on him from the wall. Notwithstanding this watch, another

33.text: shaman succeeds in spiriting him away. This one also has a keˊlᴇ-wife of

34.text: his own, but he takes also that of his vanquished rival; and now the faces

35.text: of his two keˊlᴇ-wives watch over him from both walls while his human wife

36.text: cuts meat for his meal. He also sleeps very comfortably with his three wives.
